voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
To us, Jesus is very God of very God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father. That is our creed's own answer, confessed at baptism and fought over for a century. He is the one by whom all things were made, who for us and for our salvation came down from heaven, was made flesh, and became man. He suffered, was buried, and rose again on the third day. 

Leo's own Tome, read aloud at the council that closed our era, says why the precision mattered: He who is true God is also true man. In this union there is no deception and no mixture. Each form does what is proper to it with the cooperation of the other: the Word performs what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carries out what belongs to the flesh. One person, two natures, unconfused. True God, so that what he gives is truly God's to give. True man, so that the death he died could be ours and the victory he won could be God's.

We did not write devotional memoirs about him. We wrote definitions, and we wrote them the way people write what they are prepared to be exiled over.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
He came down from heaven, was incarnate by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary, and was made man. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate, suffered, and was buried. On the third day he rose again, according to the Scriptures. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

Leo's Tome says what the doing means: the Word performs what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carries out what belongs to the flesh. One of them gleams with miracles, the other succumbs to injuries. The Word does not withdraw from equality with the Father's glory, yet the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race. So the death is real - ours, fully - and the victory is real - God's, fully - because both natures act in the one person who is both.

That is what we confessed. What it meant in any single believer's daily life, our record does not tell us. We have the church's public testimony, not its private one.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
Of one substance with the Father. The Nicene word that binds the Son to the Father as one and the same being. Not merely like God - sharing the very being that makes the Father God.

The word itself does not come from scripture, and that was the fight. For two imperial reigns our own establishment refused it and confessed instead that the Son is homoios - like the Father, as the scriptures say, with no further word about shared being. The Homoian formula refused both 'of one substance' and 'of a different substance' as words scripture does not use. When Nicaea first spoke the word in 325, even one of the council's own bishops hesitated before signing. Socrates records that Eusebius of Caesarea held back, thought carefully about whether he ought to accept the statement, then finally agreed and signed with everyone else. He wrote home explaining the word homoousios so that no one could question his motives because of his earlier hesitation.

So the question was never closed by pretending no one doubted. It was settled by a century of councils making the words exact enough to bind.

glosses.translational_sense: "Did a council vote Jesus into being God?" - the real history is harder: the disputed word was argued, enforced, reversed, and re-enforced across half a century, in both directions, with the state's weight behind whichever confession the reigning emperor held.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
We believed it because the apostles' testimony, handed down through scripture and confession, said so - and because a century of argument had shown us that anything less cost us everything. If the Son is not truly God, of one substance with the Father, then what he gives is not God's to give. If he is not truly man, then the death he died is not ours. Leo's Tome puts it plainly: each nature does what belongs to it in one person, so that the death could be ours and the victory could be God's. We needed both to be true, or the cross saves no one.

The definitions were not abstractions. They were tested by exile. Bishops signed the creed at Nicaea, then some were removed under the next emperor for holding it. Others were exiled under a different settlement. Canon 1 at Chalcedon condemns anyone who dares compose a different faith, or produce or teach or hand down a different creed. We wrote these words the way people write what they are prepared to lose their sees over.

The argument itself was the devotion. In the language we actually had, getting the words right was how we guarded what the apostles left us.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
Ambrose lived it exactly where the teaching met the cost. He was made bishop of Milan in 374, baptized and ordained within a week because the city was splitting over which confession its bishop would hold. Thirteen years later, when the imperial court demanded he surrender a basilica to the Homoian establishment, he refused. The building filled with his own people, soldiers surrounded it, and the penalties were real: merchants ordered to pay two hundred pounds of gold within three days, innocent people chained during Lent, prisons filling with tradespeople. Ambrose stayed inside and preached. His people sang psalms through the whole night. The basilica was never surrendered.

Three years after that, when the emperor ordered a massacre at Thessalonica and was not yet sorry, Ambrose did not hand him forgiveness. He barred him from the altar and waited. The emperor submitted. Forgiveness came at the end of repentance, not in place of it.

That is living it out: holding the confession at the cost of everything a city could lose, and holding the emperor himself under the same discipline the confession required of everyone.

glosses.translational_sense: Not "basilica" in the modern honorific sense of a papally-designated church - here it is the ordinary word for the great hall where the church actually met.
false_friend: a purely architectural term with no institutional weight

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
That the alliance we formed cost us something we can never get back, and we knew it even then. Before Constantine, we had bishops who shepherded a persecuted flock. After him, those same bishops were asked to settle imperial-scale disputes, and the office changed under the weight. Augustine, writing after Rome itself had fallen, said plainly what a Christian emperor's happiness was not: long reigns, peaceful deaths, sons inheriting thrones, victories over enemies. Even worshippers of demons have received those gifts, he said, and they do not belong to the kingdom of God. A Christian emperor is happy if he rules justly, fears and loves God, is slow to punish and quick to pardon, and would rather rule his own wicked desires than any nation at all. That is the standard Augustine named - after watching what Christian empire actually did.

We held basilicas against courts. We also shielded arsonists who burned a synagogue, using the same sacramental leverage. The power to refuse an emperor worked both ways. The cost of the alliance shows clearest in what we will not let you forget about us.

sources.spoken_rendering: We do not say that certain Christian emperors were happy simply because they ruled for a long time. We do not say they were happy because they died a peaceful death and left their sons to succeed them in the empire. We do not say they were happy because they defeated the enemies of the republic. We do not say they were happy because they could guard against hostile citizens who rose up against them, and crush those attempts. Even certain worshippers of demons have earned to receive these and other gifts and comforts of this sorrowful life — people who do not belong to the kingdom of God, to which Christian emperors belong. This is to be traced to the mercy of God, who does not want those who believe in him to desire such things as the highest good. But we say they are happy if they rule justly. They are happy if they are not carried away by the praise of those who give them grand honors, and by the flattery of those who greet them with excessive humility — if instead they remember that they are men. They are happy if they make their power the servant of God's majesty, using it to spread his worship as widely as possible. They are happy if they fear, love, and worship God. They are happy if they love that kingdom, where they are not afraid to have partners, more than their own. They are happy if they are slow to punish and quick to pardon. They are happy if they apply punishment as necessary for governing and defending the republic, and not to satisfy their own hatred. They are happy if they grant pardon, not so that wrongdoing goes unpunished, but in the hope that the wrongdoer may change his ways. They are happy if they balance whatever severity they are forced to decree with the gentleness of mercy and the generosity of kindness. They are happy if their indulgence is held back as much as it could have run free. They are happy if they would rather rule over their own wicked desires than over any nation at all. And they are happy if they do all these things, not out of a burning desire for empty glory, but out of love for eternal happiness — and if they do not fail to offer to the true God, who is their God, the sacrifices of humility, sorrow for sin, and prayer, for their own sins.
